- **[2026.09]**: We release **EvoOntology**, a self-evolving ontology layer for data agents that grounds semantic context in real workloads and continuously adapts through verified execution trajectories.

- **[2026.09]**: We release **SkillAdam** 🚀, an easy-to-use plugin for automatically improving the skills of your AI agents. SkillAdam integrates directly with **Codex, Claude Code, Cursor Agent, and GitHub Copilot**, with simple installation and no need for a local GPU, Docker, or a separate model API key.

**SkillAdam** makes skill optimization simple and automatic. Just provide a `SKILL.md` and describe what you want to improve. SkillAdam automatically generates relevant tasks, evaluates the current skill, proposes improvements, validates the revised version, and updates the skill when the changes pass evaluation. With a one-step installer, it works directly inside the coding agent you already use.
- **[2026.07]**: We look forward to releasing **DeepPrep**, a data-preparation companion to DeepAnalyze that turns raw tables into analysis-ready data.

**DeepPrep** is an LLM-powered agentic system for autonomous data preparation. It constructs data-preparation pipelines through execution-grounded interaction with intermediate table states and runtime feedback, helping clean, transform, and standardize raw data before downstream analysis.
- **[2026.06.15]**: We release **CoDA-Bench**, a benchmark for evaluating whether code agents can handle data-intensive analytical tasks, closely aligned with DeepAnalyze's target scenarios.

**CoDA-Bench** evaluates agents in a Linux sandbox with hundreds of data files. Given a natural-language question, an agent must discover relevant data, write executable code, and produce the final answer. It provides a benchmark setting for the same type of data discovery and code-execution challenges targeted by DeepAnalyze.

Distributed sites have gained much attention lately with systems such as ZeroNet and IPFS, which seem to improve on older systems like Freenet.
* Update your site using the Mutable Torrents extension (BEP46) and let your users know about site updates via the DHT network.
* Build interactive sites that are queryable on demand using the sqltorrent technique. Things like search engines, or complex browsable experiences are possible.

* Hosting your site is as simple as seeding a torrent. No need to buy a domain name or a hosting server. You can easily host your torrent site on your home network and let users visiting your site help you with the hosting.
* Since you control your address (public key), which is broadcast via the DHT, it's much harder for governments and institution to block the content you're sharing.

* Via sqltorrent you drive your users experience by letting them only downloading pieces of the torrent that are relevant to the users' interaction. Essentially you could create a search engine, and program interactions so that submissions of a search form result in queries to the underlying SQLite database - which prioritizes pieces based on the query.
* Read only sites for now. ZeroNet seems to have a solution to this problem but I'm not convinced yet.
* Your site doesn't have a pretty name. Sharing your public key can be much harder than sharing the name of a DNS site.

* No standards for doing distributed sites. Many different solutions (IPFS, ZeroNet, Freenet, etc..). TorrentPeek at least follows most of the BitTorrent specifications (using the powerful libtorrent library) and provides unique SQL querying capabilities.

**`REPOSITORY.md`** is the map: every directory, all deploy targets, and which areas are engine versus hosted product. Read it before the layout below surprises you.
|`apps/web`|The Next.js app: UI, auth, command acceptance, synchronous reads.|
|`apps/landing`|The public site (launchstack.app): landing, pricing, contact, deployment guide. No database, no auth; **not** part of any self-hosted deployment.|
|`apps/worker`|The durable workflow coordinator — consumes the ingestion outbox and hosts the background jobs (ADR-003).|
|`packages/`|The bricks: persistence, model calls, orchestration, conversion, indexing, retrieval, shared tools and independent clients. See `packages/README.md` for the spine and side packages.|

|`services/`|Compute services — document-converter (Node), transcription and adeu-ai-docs-editing (Python). Not part of the pnpm workspace; each manages its own dependencies.|

|`@launchstack/orchestration`|unpublished|Transactional outbox, source lifecycle, worker tick and stage ports.|
|`@launchstack/conversion`|unpublished|Sources to `EvidenceDocument`: document conversion, OCR, transcription and archive expansion.|
|`@launchstack/indexing`|unpublished|Chunking, embeddings, entity extraction, Neo4j sync and the document-ingestion pipeline.|
|`@launchstack/tools`|unpublished|Shared capabilities composed by verticals: company context, web research, social publishing, grants and stage execution.|

`createEngine(config)` opens the database pool and registers the database, storage, metering and Neo4j slots, plus credits and RAG ports when supplied. Several subsystems need **separate** registration calls — `apps/web/src/server/engine.ts` makes seven: the host-local `configureAppChatModels`, `configureEmbeddingIndexRegistry`, `configureCompanyEmbeddingDefaults`, `configureProviders`, `configureSecretBox`, `configureOcr` and `configureEntityExtraction`. The chat helper loads the app's YAML and registers the same `config.llm.chat` that `createEngine` applies; a custom host can pass a chat config directly without that app-local helper. Slots are read lazily, so register them before a subsystem is first *used*.

`@launchstack/engine` is the one-install aggregate: `createEngine(CoreConfig)` assembles the engine spine and re-exports selected runtime, database, conversion, indexing and orchestration APIs. Import model, OCR, embedding and retrieval APIs from their owning bricks' public subpaths; individual bricks can also be consumed separately. CI checks the declared publishable subpaths under plain Node ESM (`scripts/ci/check-package-exports.mjs`). The engine package reads no `process.env` (lint-enforced) — configuration arrives through `CoreConfig`, typed ports and separate `configure*` hooks; `apps/web/src/server/engine.ts` is the reference composition root.

**Library**: A quicker and simpler short-term fix is to use a bundled native PHP library such as php7-mysql-shim. Instead of converting code (e.g., `mysql_connect()` to `mysqli_connect()`) it uses `ext/mysqli` to define `ext/mysql` functions in PHP. Much easier but more of a short-term fix. Although `php7-mysql-shim` contains PHP 7 in the name, it works with older PHP versions but only if `ext/mysql` is not installed on your system.
**Convertor**: The Rector tool is popular and maintained; and it includes tools to convert ext/mysql code to ext/mysqli code. See its mysqltomysqli rules.

With `short-open-tag` disabled, short tags (<? and <?=) are essentially ignored due to how the `tokenizer` extension works. So, if you use the likes of <? (instead of <?php) then enable `short-open-tag` before executing the conversion otherwise that PHP code will be ignored (not converted). For details, see issue #16.

The php7-mysql-shim PHP library defines all mysql_ functions for you, so simply include it (a single PHP file) and your code should work without a need to convert. It uses ext/mysqli and works fine in PHP 5.3 or greater. There are pros and cons to each approach.
